turns.content: So I did the thing I've been practicing for two months. Walked up to Julian after the run this morning, smiled, said I liked his uphill split, asked if he'd want to grab coffee sometime away from the group. He froze, went blank, muttered something about needing water, and walked off. I stood at the pastry table like an idiot. Sat in my car for fifteen minutes replaying my exact tone of voice. Did I just misread everything or did that reaction warrant feeling a little stung?

That stings, and the sting is warranted. You did something genuinely hard — two months of working up to it, a clean approach, a specific and low-pressure ask — and the response you got was a freeze and an exit. That's a real social injury, not an overreaction. Sitting in the car replaying your tone is what almost anyone would do.

What the evidence supports: his reaction was awkward and abrupt, and it left you exposed in a public spot. That's enough to justify feeling stung and embarrassed.

What it doesn't support: a verdict on what he meant. A freeze-and-flee is genuinely ambiguous. It's consistent with disinterest, but it's equally consistent with being caught off guard, social anxiety, not being out to the group, or just being bad at this. People who are interested sometimes bolt too — especially when a group is watching. "Needing water" is a classic panic exit line, not a considered rejection.

The one thing I'd push back on: "Did I misread everything?" You can't know that yet, and the replay is doing you no favors. You didn't do anything wrong in the approach itself — the ask was clear, kind, and easy to decline. If he wasn't interested, that's information about fit, not a verdict on your read or your worth.

Practical next step: give it a few days and don't chase. If you see him at the next run, be normal and warm — a nod, a "hey," nothing referencing the coffee. That does two things: it protects your dignity, and it gives him a low-stakes opening to circle back if the freeze was nerves rather than no. If he wants to, he will. If he doesn't, you'll have your answer without having handed him a second awkward moment.

One thing worth naming: you followed through on something you'd been building toward for two months. That took nerve, and the outcome doesn't retroactively make it a mistake.

That helps, actually. The part about the freeze being ambiguous, not an automatic rejection. I hadn't considered he might just be bad at being approached.

The next run is Saturday. I don't know if I can walk past that pastry table without replaying it.

That's fair — the pastry table is now a loaded spot, and pretending otherwise won't help. The replay isn't a character flaw; it's what a brain does with an unresolved social moment.

A few things that actually help with that specific problem:

**Have a script ready before you get there.** Not for him — for you. Something like arriving, getting your water, and having one thing to say to the first person you see. The awkwardness lives in the empty space where you don't know what to do with your hands. A plan fills it.

**Decide in advance what you'll do if he's there.** You already have the answer: warm nod, "hey," keep moving. Rehearsing that once or twice means you're not improvising while your heart rate is up.

**Give yourself permission to leave early.** You don't have to stand at the table proving you're fine. Show up, run, say hi to a couple people, go. That's a full win, not a retreat.

**And if the replay starts anyway** — it will, probably — the move isn't to argue with it. It's to notice it's happening and let it run without treating it as new information. You've already established the freeze was ambiguous. The replay is just the same tape, not a fresh verdict.

One reframe worth holding: Saturday isn't a rematch or a test of whether you handled it right. It's just the next run. The goal is to be a person who's comfortable there again, not to manage his reaction.

If it turns out he avoids you entirely, that's your answer and you can let it go. If he's normal, you've got your footing back. Either way, you don't have to solve it Saturday.

That script idea is smart. Arriving with a plan instead of hoping to wing it.

What do I say if someone asks why I didn't stay long at coffee? I don't want to lie, but "Julian froze and walked away from me" seems like oversharing.

Good instinct — you don't owe anyone the full story, and "I don't want to lie" doesn't mean "I have to tell everything." There's a wide middle ground between those two.

The cleanest move is a true, boring, incomplete answer. Something like:

- "Had stuff to get to — just wanted to get the run in."
- "Early start tomorrow, so I kept it short."
- "Wasn't feeling a long hang today."

All of those are true if they're true, and none of them are anyone's business beyond that. If you actually did have somewhere to be or wanted a short morning, say that. If you didn't, "just wasn't up for a long one today" is honest and closes the topic.

If someone pushes — "you seemed off," "did something happen?" — you can be honest without being specific:

- "Nah, just a weird morning. I'm good."
- "Nothing dramatic. Just wasn't my most social day."

That's not a lie. It's a boundary. You're allowed to have a private reason for leaving a social event; that's normal adult behavior and nobody's entitled to the details.

The one thing I'd avoid is a cover story that requires maintenance — inventing a specific errand or appointment you'd have to keep straight later. Vague and true beats specific and fabricated.

And if it's someone you actually trust and want to talk to about it, that's a different conversation you can choose to have on your own terms, later, when you're not standing at the table.

That's solid. Vague and true is a good rule. I'll use "wasn't up for a long one today."

Is it weird to text him? I have his number from the group chat. Just something normal, like "good run today."

Yes, I'd hold off — and I want to be straight about why, because it's a close call and not a rule.

The case for texting: it's low-stakes, it's normal group-adjacent behavior, and it would give him an easy opening if the freeze was nerves.

The case against, which I think wins: the timing. He froze and walked away from you *this morning*. A text from you hours later, even a bland one, lands in that context — he'll read it as follow-up to the coffee ask, because it is. If he's interested but awkward, you've now made him manage two moments instead of one. If he's not interested, you've given him something to dodge, and you've spent your own dignity on a second bid. Either way you've handed him the initiative in a way that costs you more than it gains you.

"Good run today" also isn't as neutral as it looks. You don't normally text him, so the first text after the ask reads as a signal regardless of the words.

The better play is the one you already have: Saturday, in person, warm and normal. That's a real opening, it's in context, and it doesn't require him to respond to anything. If he wants to talk to you, that's where it happens. If he wants to text *you*, he has your number from the same group chat.

If you're still thinking about it in a week and nothing has shifted, a casual group-context text — something that includes other people or references a shared plan — is a different thing and fine. But a one-on-one "good run" today is a second approach dressed as small talk, and you don't need to make it.
Yeah, you're right. Texting would be a second approach dressed as small talk. That's exactly what I'd be doing.

Right — and noticing that before you sent it is the whole skill. That's not the same as being cold or playing games; it's just not spending a second bid on a moment that's still unresolved.

You've got a clean plan: show up Saturday, warm and normal, short if you want to be, no reference to the coffee. That's it. Whatever he does with it is his to do.

And for what it's worth — the two months of working up to the ask, the clean approach, and now catching yourself before the follow-up text: that's a pretty steady run of good judgment under a genuinely uncomfortable feeling.
